cases.reply: Above 10,000 MSL in Class E airspace, the VFR cloud clearance requirement is "clear of clouds." The rule is 14 CFR §91.155(a), which states that no person may operate an aircraft under VFR closer than 500 feet to the surface, except over open water or sparsely populated areas, then not below 1,000 feet AGL. For Class E airspace above 10,000 MSL, "clear of clouds" means the aircraft must see at least 1 statute mile horizontally and maintain the required visibility and distance from clouds.

To enter Class B airspace as a VFR pilot, you need an explicit ATC clearance — "cleared into the Bravo" — before entering. You must also maintain a Mode C transponder and be on the appropriate frequency for communication with ATC. The clearance will specify the authorized altitude for your flight in Class B airspace. The rule is in 14 CFR §91.131(a) and the phraseology is defined in JO 7110.65.

- **FAA Order JO 7110.65, Para 2-1-18, Operational Requests.**
- **FAA Order JO 7110.65, Para 2-4-22, Airspace Classes.**

**Phraseology:** "Cleared into the Bravo," "Cleared through the Bravo," or "Cleared to enter the Bravo airspace."

- **AIM 4-4-7 (Pilot Responsibility upon Clearance Issuance)** for more details.

Above 3,000 feet AGL, the VFR cruising altitude requirements are as follows: 500 feet for the first 2,500 feet, and 1,000 feet for each additional 2,500 feet, per 14 CFR §91.159. For example, between 3,000 and 5,500 feet MSL, maintain 3,000 feet; between 5,500 and 8,000 feet MSL, maintain 5,500 feet. The rule applies to level cruising flight and excludes holding patterns of 2 minutes or less and turning maneuvers. The exact altitudes are in the table of 14 CFR §91.159, and the AIM provides a pilot-facing summary.

14 CFR §91.113 — When two aircraft of the same category are converging at approximately the same altitude, the aircraft to the right has the right-of-way. Specifically, according to 14 CFR §91.113(d):

- If the aircraft are of the same category, the one to the right has the right-of-way. Maintain vigilance to ensure your aircraft is to the right.

The key preflight actions per 14 CFR §91.103 are:

- Become familiar with all available information concerning the flight.
- For IFR or distant flights, include weather reports, fuel requirements, and known traffic delays.
- For any flight, check runway lengths and takeoff/landing distances:
  - For civil aircraft with an approved flight manual, use the data within.
  - For other aircraft, use other reliable information considering airport elevation, runway slope, aircraft weight, and wind/temperature conditions.

These actions ensure the pilot is well-prepared and informed.

Below 18,000 MSL, set your altimeter to the current reported altimeter setting of a station within 100 nautical miles, per 14 CFR §91.121(a)(1). If no such station is available, use the current reported setting of an appropriate station or the elevation of the departure airport if the aircraft is not equipped with a radio. The exact procedure is in 14 CFR §91.121 and further explained in the AIM and PHAK.
Above 10,000 MSL in Class E airspace, a Mode C transponder is required. Below 10,000 MSL, no specific transponder requirement exists. The rule is 14 CFR §91.215.

The pilot in command has final authority over the aircraft's operation and safety. Per 14 CFR §91.3(a), if ATC issues a clearance that would violate this, the pilot must request an amended clearance to ensure compliance. Don't know other paths to try.

- Altitude assignments
- Heading and vector assignments
- Speed instructions
- Hold-short instructions
- Runway-crossing clearances

The full call sign goes first so the controller can match the readback to the flight. Partial readbacks invite misidentification; don't economize.

— AIM 4-4-7

To avoid wake turbulence behind a large jet as a student pilot, follow these steps:

- Rotate before the large jet's rotation point.
- Climb above the jet’s path.
- Stay upwind of the jet’s track.
- Follow AIM 7-4-6 for detailed procedures.

The AIM provides specific guidance on managing your flight path to stay clear of the vortices.

An IFR flight must file an alternate airport if the weather at the primary destination is expected to be below the minimums for the planned approach. The rule is in 14 CFR §91.167. The FAA identifies three critical situations:

- When the MDA or landing visibility for all instrument approaches is higher than forecasted.
- When the weather is worse than forecasted, and there’s insufficient fuel to reach a suitable airport.
- When the weather is worse than forecasted, and the aircraft can’t climb to the required altitude.

The rule is also in 14 CFR §91.169(a)(2), which requires an alternate unless:

- The destination has a standard or special instrument approach.
- Weather reports or forecasts show at least 2,000 feet ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility for at least 1 hour before and after the estimated arrival.

So, an alternate must be filed if the weather is expected to be below the minimums and the conditions in 14 CFR §91.169 are not met. The rule is in 14 CFR §91.169.

Takeoff minimums are not explicitly required by 14 CFR §91.103, but pilots should consider weather conditions and maintain VFR during takeoff and climbout. For IFR operations, ensure you can meet en route minimums and have an alternate airport. For VFR operations, basic weather minimums are in 14 CFR §91.155. Some airports have nonstandard departure procedures; check the FAA/DoD IAP charts. Entering Class B airspace requires an explicit clearance per 14 CFR §91.131. The AIM and IAP charts provide more detail. Don't know specific takeoff minimums; check 14 CFR §91.155 and the AIM.

When a missed approach is initiated, follow these steps:

- Execute the published missed approach procedure without delay.
- Climb to a safe altitude before proceeding.
- Contact ATC to report the missed approach and request further clearance.
- Consider weather, aircraft performance, and traffic before initiating.
- Coordinate with ATC for any changes or alternative actions.
- Follow the appropriate procedures as directed.

The rule is 14 CFR §91.135. The AIM covers this in chapter 7.

The minimum en-route altitude (MEA) for IFR operations is defined in 14 CFR §91.177. It must be at or above the minimum IFR altitude (MIA) for the route. The MIA is defined as follows:

- In mountainous areas: 2,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 4 nautical miles of the route.
- In other areas: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 4 nautical miles of the route.
- As otherwise authorized by the Administrator or assigned by ATC.

The exact MEA for a specific route can be found on aeronautical charts or in the route procedures published by the FAA. For more detail, refer to FAA Order JO 7110.65, Chapter 5, Section 6, Para 5-6-1, and the Pilot/Controller Glossary (PCG) for definitions and procedures.

The clearance limit is the fix, point, or location that bounds your clearance. You're authorized to fly to it, not past it. When you reach the limit, hold as published if there's a charted hold, or as directed by ATC if the clearance carried holding instructions. ATC normally issues an Expect Further Clearance (EFC) time. For more details, refer to `AIM 5-3-8` and `14 CFR §91.185`.

14 CFR §91.185(b) and (c) cover this. If you lose two-way radio communication in IMC on an IFR flight plan, continue the flight according to the last ATC clearance. If being radar vectored, follow the direct route to the fix, route, or airway specified. In the absence of an assigned route, follow the route advised by ATC. If no route or clearance, follow the route filed in the flight plan. Maintain the highest altitude or flight level as specified in the last clearance. Expect an EFC time. If VFR conditions are encountered, land as soon as practicable. The rule is in 14 CFR §91.185(b) and (c); the AIM 6-4-1 and JO 7110.65 §10-4-4 provide details. Always check current publications for updates.

An aircraft's approach category is based on its speed in the landing configuration at maximum gross landing weight. Categories are as follows:

- **Category A:** Speed less than 91 knots.
- **Category B:** Speed 91 knots or more but less than 121 knots.
- **Category C:** Speed 121 knots or more but less than 141 knots.
- **Category D:** Speed 141 knots or more but less than 166 knots.
- **Category E:** Speed 166 knots or more.

These categories determine approach minimums and wake turbulence separation. If an aircraft is circling at a speed above the upper limit of a category, use the higher category's minimums. For example, an aircraft in Category A circling at 95 knots must use Category B minimums.

The rules are in 14 CFR Part 97.

VFR-on-top is a special clearance allowing an aircraft to climb through clouds and maintain VFR at or above the cruising altitude or flight level. You can request this clearance under these conditions:

- The pilot must specifically request "VFR-on-top."
- Inform the pilot of the cloud top height or that no top reports are available.
- Ensure separation from other traffic by issuing an alternative clearance if necessary.
- Re-clear the aircraft to maintain VFR-on-top when they report reaching it.

Phrasing:
- "CLIMB TO AND REPORT REACHING VFR-ON-TOP, " or "TOPS REPORTED (altitude), " or "NO TOPS REPORTS. " If not on top at (altitude), maintain (altitude) and advise.
- "MAINTAIN VFR-ON-TOP."

Restrictions:
- Do not clear an aircraft to maintain VFR-on-top between sunset and sunrise to separate holding aircraft or en route traffic unless specific IFR vertical separation is ensured.

Reference: JO 7110.65 §7-3-1 (VFR-On-Top — VFR-ON-TOP)

The instrument currency requirements for IFR operations are in 14 CFR §61.57. Here’s a summary:

- To be current, a pilot must complete a flight review or an instrument proficiency check within the last 6 months.
- A flight review must be in an appropriate aircraft and cover the areas of operation in the applicable Airman Certification Standards.
- An instrument proficiency check is required if the instrument experience is more than 6 months old. It must also cover the areas of operation and can be conducted in an aircraft, flight simulator, or flight training device.
- For certain aircraft types, like the Mitsubishi MU–2B series, the flight review must include special emphasis items and all items from the Training Course Final Phase Check.
- Initial/transition, requalification, or recurrent training under 14 CFR §91.1705 meets the requirements if at least 1 hour was in the appropriate aircraft or an approved simulator.

For more details, see 14 CFR §61.57 and the Airman Certification Standards.

— 14 CFR §61.56

You can descend below the MDA or DA on an instrument approach only if you meet the conditions in 14 CFR §91.175(c). Specifically, you must be able to continuously maintain a position from which a normal rate of descent can be made to land on the intended runway. This means:

- You can see and land on the runway at a normal rate of descent using normal maneuvers.
- You do not need to go around.

The key points are:

- Visibility of the runway environment.
- Safe landing at a normal rate of descent.

For more details, see AIM §5-4-7.

No, you cannot cancel an IFR clearance while in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC). The rule is in 14 CFR §91.153. You must maintain the IFR clearance until you are in VFR conditions or have landed. To cancel, notify ATC when in VFR conditions, then follow the VFR procedures, including changing frequencies, setting the VFR radar code, and flying the appropriate VFR altitude or flight level. The AIM 5-1-15 covers this: "CANCEL MY IFR FLIGHT PLAN" to the controller when in VFR outside Class A airspace.
